name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q01 - Force on a charge moving perpendicular to a magnetic field

questiontext.text: A proton carrying a charge of \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) enters a uniform magnetic field of \(0.25\text{ T}\) with a speed of \(4.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\) at right angles to the direction of the field. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the proton?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Charge of the proton, \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.25\text{ T}\).
Velocity of the proton, \(v = 4.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Angle between velocity vector and magnetic field vector, \(\theta = 90^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnetic field is uniform and static. Relativistic effects are neglected since \(v \ll c\). The force magnitude is scalar.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic Lorentz force on a moving charge is given by:
\[F = q v B \sin\theta\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[F = (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) \times (4.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}) \times (0.25\text{ T}) \times \sin(90^\circ)\]
Since \(\sin(90^\circ) = 1\):
\[F = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{6} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The units \(\text{C} \cdot \text{m s}^{-1} \cdot \text{T} = \text{N}\) are consistent.
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the proton is \(1.6 \times 10^{-13}\text{ N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q02 - Magnetic field at the center of a circular coil

questiontext.text: A circular coil of wire consisting of \(50\) turns, each of radius \(8.0\text{ cm}\), carries a current of \(0.40\text{ A}\). What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of the coil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of turns in the circular coil, \(N = 50\).
Radius of the coil, \(R = 8.0\text{ cm} = 0.08\text{ m}\).
Current carried by the coil, \(I = 0.40\text{ A}\).
Permeability of free space, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The coil is closely wound such that all turns can be considered to have the same radius \(R\) and lie in the same plane.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field at the centre of a flat circular coil of \(N\) turns is given by Biot-Savart law as:
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values:
\[B = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 50 \times 0.40\text{ A}}{2 \times 0.08\text{ m}}\]
Simplify the numerator and denominator:
\[B = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 20}{0.16} = \frac{80\pi \times 10^{-7}}{0.16} = 500\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\]
Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[B = 500 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-7} = 1.5708 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} \approx 1.57 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dimensional analysis yields tesla (\(\text{T}\)), and the numerical magnitude is physically sound.
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of the coil is \(1.57 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q03 - Magnetic field inside a long solenoid

questiontext.text: A closely wound solenoid of length \(0.5\text{ m}\) has \(500\) turns of wire. If it carries a current of \(2.0\text{ A}\), what is the magnetic field inside the solenoid near its centre?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of the solenoid, \(L = 0.5\text{ m}\).
Total number of turns, \(N = 500\).
Current, \(I = 2.0\text{ A}\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The solenoid is considered sufficiently long so that end effects can be neglected near the centre.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field inside an ideal long solenoid near its centre is given by Ampere's circuital law as:
\[B = \mu_0 n I\]
where \(n = \frac{N}{L}\) is the number of turns per unit length.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the turn density \(n\):
\[n = \frac{500}{0.5\text{ m}} = 1000\text{ turns m}^{-1}\]
Substitute \(n\) and \(I\) into the field equation:
\[B = (4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times (1000\text{ m}^{-1}) \times (2.0\text{ A})\]
\[B = 8\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\]
With \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[B = 8 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-4} = 2.513 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T} \approx 2.51 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The unit is tesla and the order of magnitude corresponds to typical laboratory solenoids.
Therefore, the magnetic field inside the solenoid near its centre is \(2.51 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q04 - Magnetic dipole moment of a flat circular loop

questiontext.text: A circular coil of \(20\) turns and radius \(10\text{ cm}\) carries a steady current of \(3.0\text{ A}\). What is the magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment associated with the coil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of turns, \(N = 20\).
Radius of the coil, \(R = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\).
Current, \(I = 3.0\text{ A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The coil is planar. The magnetic moment vector points perpendicular to the plane of the coil according to the right-hand grip rule.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment \(m\) of a current-carrying planar coil is given by:
\[m = N I A\]
where \(A = \pi R^2\) is the cross-sectional area enclosed by each turn.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the area \(A\):
\[A = \pi R^2 = \pi (0.10\text{ m})^2 = 0.01\pi\text{ m}^2\]
Compute the magnetic dipole moment:
\[m = 20 \times (3.0\text{ A}) \times (0.01\pi\text{ m}^2) = 0.60\pi\text{ A m}^2\]
Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[m = 0.60 \times 3.1416 = 1.88496\text{ A m}^2 \approx 1.88\text{ A m}^2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \(\text{A} \cdot \text{m}^2\), which matches the SI unit of magnetic moment.
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment associated with the coil is \(1.88\text{ A m}^{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q05 - Force on a straight current carrying conductor in magnetic field

questiontext.text: A straight wire of length \(1.5\text{ m}\) carries a current of \(2.0\text{ A}\) in a direction making an angle of \(30^\circ\) with a uniform magnetic field of \(0.40\text{ T}\). What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on the wire?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of the conductor, \(l = 1.5\text{ m}\).
Current in the conductor, \(I = 2.0\text{ A}\).
Angle with the magnetic field, \(\theta = 30^\circ\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.40\text{ T}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The conductor is straight and placed entirely within a uniform magnetic field.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic force on a straight current-carrying wire is given by:
\[F = I l B \sin\theta\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[F = (2.0\text{ A}) \times (1.5\text{ m}) \times (0.40\text{ T}) \times \sin(30^\circ)\]
Since \(\sin(30^\circ) = 0.5\):
\[F = 3.0 \times 0.40 \times 0.5 = 0.60\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The product yields newtons correctly. At \(\theta = 30^\circ\), the force is half the maximum force \(1.20\text{ N}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic force on the wire is \(0.60\text{ N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q06 - Magnetic field at a distance from a long straight wire

questiontext.text: A long, straight horizontal wire carries a current of \(35\text{ A}\). What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at a perpendicular distance of \(20\text{ cm}\) from the wire?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current carried by the straight wire, \(I = 35\text{ A}\).
Perpendicular distance from the wire, \(r = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m}\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The wire is straight, infinitely long compared to \(r\), and surrounded by vacuum or air.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From Ampere's circuital law, the magnetic field at distance \(r\) from a long straight current-carrying wire is:
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[B = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 35\text{ A}}{2\pi \times 0.20\text{ m}}\]
Simplify the factor \(\frac{4\pi}{2\pi} = 2\):
\[B = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 35}{0.20} = \frac{70 \times 10^{-7}}{0.20} = 350 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T} = 3.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are in tesla and \(35\,\mu\text{T}\) is physically typical for this current and distance.
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field at the given distance is \(3.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q07 - Force per unit length between two parallel current carrying wires

questiontext.text: Two long, straight parallel wires separated by a distance of \(10\text{ cm}\) in air carry currents of \(4.0\text{ A}\) and \(5.0\text{ A}\) in the same direction. What is the magnitude of the force per unit length exerted by one wire on the other?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current in the first wire, \(I_1 = 4.0\text{ A}\).
Current in the second wire, \(I_2 = 5.0\text{ A}\).
Separation distance between the wires, \(d = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The wires are infinitely long, parallel, and placed in vacuum/air. Parallel currents in the same direction attract each other.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnitude of the magnetic force per unit length \(f\) between two parallel current-carrying wires is:
\[f = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[f = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 4.0 \times 5.0}{2\pi \times 0.10}\]
Cancel \(2\pi\) into \(4\pi\) to get \(2\):
\[f = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20.0}{0.10} = \frac{40.0 \times 10^{-7}}{0.10} = 400 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N m}^{-1} = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N m}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The resulting unit \(\text{N m}^{-1}\) is correct for force per unit length.
Therefore, the magnitude of the force per unit length exerted by one wire on the other is \(4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N m}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q08 - Radius of circular path of electron in uniform magnetic field

questiontext.text: An electron of mass \(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\) and charge magnitude \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of \(500\text{ V}\) and then enters perpendicularly into a uniform magnetic field of \(0.20\text{ T}\). What is the radius of the circular path traced by the electron?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of electron, \(m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\).
Charge of electron, \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
Accelerating potential difference, \(V = 500\text{ V}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.20\text{ T}\).
Entrance angle, \(\theta = 90^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Kinetic energy gained by the electron is \(K = qV\). The speed is non-relativistic.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The radius \(r\) of circular motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field is:
\[r = \frac{m v}{q B} = \frac{p}{q B}\]
Since \(K = \frac{p^2}{2m} = qV\), the momentum is \(p = \sqrt{2mqV}\).
Thus:
\[r = \frac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{qB} = \frac{1}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2mV}{q}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate momentum \(p\):
\[p = \sqrt{2 \times (9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) \times (500\text{ V})}\]
\[p = \sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 1.6 \times 500 \times 10^{-50}} = \sqrt{14560 \times 10^{-50}} = \sqrt{1.456 \times 10^{-46}} \approx 1.2066 \times 10^{-23}\text{ kg m s}^{-1}\]
Now compute the radius \(r\):
\[r = \frac{p}{qB} = \frac{1.2066 \times 10^{-23}\text{ kg m s}^{-1}}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) \times (0.20\text{ T})}\]
\[r = \frac{1.2066 \times 10^{-23}}{3.2 \times 10^{-20}} = 0.37707 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} = 3.77 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The resulting unit is metres and the value is sub-millimetre, as expected for high magnetic field and light electrons.
Therefore, the radius of the circular path traced by the electron is \(3.77 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q09 - Pitch of helical path of a charged particle in magnetic field

questiontext.text: A proton of mass \(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\) and charge \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) enters a uniform magnetic field of \(0.50\text{ T}\) with a speed of \(2.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\) at an angle of \(60^\circ\) with the magnetic field lines. What is the pitch of the helical path traced by the proton?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of proton, \(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\).
Charge of proton, \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
Speed of proton, \(v = 2.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.50\text{ T}\).
Angle with field, \(\theta = 60^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The velocity resolves into two components: parallel to the field \(v_\parallel = v\cos\theta\), and perpendicular to the field \(v_\perp = v\sin\theta\). The parallel component remains unchanged while the perpendicular component undergoes uniform circular motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The time period of one revolution in the circular plane is:
\[T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}\]
The pitch \(p\) of the helix is the linear distance advanced along the field in one time period:
\[p = v_\parallel T = (v\cos\theta) \left(\frac{2\pi m}{qB}\right)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the time period \(T\):
\[T = \frac{2\pi \times (1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg})}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) \times (0.50\text{ T})} = \frac{3.34\pi \times 10^{-27}}{0.80 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.175\pi \times 10^{-8}\text{ s} \approx 1.3116 \times 10^{-7}\text{ s}\]
Calculate the parallel velocity component:
\[v_\parallel = v\cos(60^\circ) = (2.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}) \times 0.5 = 1.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\]
Calculate the pitch \(p\):
\[p = v_\parallel T = (1.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}) \times (1.3116 \times 10^{-7}\text{ s}) = 0.13116\text{ m} \approx 1.31 \times 10^{-1}\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The pitch is in metres and has positive physical length.
Therefore, the pitch of the helical path traced by the proton is \(1.31 \times 10^{-1}\text{ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q10 - Shunt resistance to convert galvanometer into ammeter

questiontext.text: A galvanometer has a resistance of \(12\text{ }\Omega\) and the meter shows full scale deflection for a current of \(3.0\text{ mA}\). How should it be modified to convert it into an ammeter of range \(0\) to \(6.0\text{ A}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Galvanometer resistance, \(G = 12\text{ }\Omega\).
Current for full scale deflection, \(I_g = 3.0\text{ mA} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}\).
Required maximum current range, \(I = 6.0\text{ A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
To measure a larger current without burning the coil, a low resistance (shunt) \(S\) must be connected in parallel with the galvanometer coil.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Since the galvanometer and shunt are connected in parallel, potential difference across both is identical:
\[I_g G = (I - I_g) S \implies S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[I - I_g = 6.0\text{ A} - 0.003\text{ A} = 5.997\text{ A}\]
Compute the required shunt resistance \(S\):
\[S = \frac{(3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}) \times 12\text{ }\Omega}{5.997\text{ A}} = \frac{0.036}{5.997}\text{ }\Omega \approx 0.006003\text{ }\Omega = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ }\Omega\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The shunt resistance is much smaller than the galvanometer coil resistance, allowing practically all the current to bypass the galvanometer.
Therefore, the required modification is a shunt resistance of \(6.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ }\Omega\text{ in parallel}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q11 - Series resistance to convert galvanometer into voltmeter

questiontext.text: A galvanometer of resistance \(25\text{ }\Omega\) gives full scale deflection with a current of \(2.0\text{ mA}\). What value of series resistance is required to convert it into a voltmeter reading up to \(10\text{ V}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Galvanometer resistance, \(G = 25\text{ }\Omega\).
Full scale deflection current, \(I_g = 2.0\text{ mA} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}\).
Desired voltage range, \(V = 10\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
To measure a high voltage, a large resistance \(R\) is connected in series with the galvanometer so that the total voltage drops across the series combination when current \(I_g\) passes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From Ohm's law applied to the series combination:
\[V = I_g (G + R) \implies R = \frac{V}{I_g} - G\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the total resistance required:
\[R_{\text{total}} = \frac{V}{I_g} = \frac{10\text{ V}}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}} = 5000\text{ }\Omega\]
Subtract the internal resistance of the galvanometer:
\[R = 5000\text{ }\Omega - 25\text{ }\Omega = 4975\text{ }\Omega\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The required series resistance is positive and significantly larger than \(G\).
Therefore, the value of series resistance required is \(4975\text{ }\Omega\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q12 - Change in current and voltage sensitivity with coil parameters

questiontext.text: A moving coil galvanometer has \(N\) turns and resistance \(R\). If the number of turns is doubled to \(2N\) using wire of the same material and cross-sectional area (so the resistance also doubles to \(2R\)), by what factor does its voltage sensitivity change?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial number of turns \(= N\), initial resistance \(= R\).
Final number of turns \(= N' = 2N\), final resistance \(= R' = 2R\).
Magnetic field \(B\), coil area \(A\), and restoring torsion constant \(k\) remain constant.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Current sensitivity is defined as deflection per unit current, \(S_i = \frac{\phi}{I}\).
Voltage sensitivity is defined as deflection per unit voltage, \(S_v = \frac{\phi}{V}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
At equilibrium, deflecting torque equals restoring torque:
\[N I A B = k \phi \implies \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{N A B}{k}\]
Using \(V = I R\):
\[S_v = \frac{\phi}{V} = \frac{\phi}{I R} = \frac{N A B}{k R}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the new parameters into the expression for voltage sensitivity \(S_v'\):
\[S_v' = \frac{N' A B}{k R'} = \frac{(2N) A B}{k (2R)} = \frac{2}{2} \left(\frac{N A B}{k R}\right) = S_v\]
The factor of \(2\) in the numerator cancels the factor of \(2\) in the denominator.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
While current sensitivity doubles when turns double, voltage sensitivity is independent of this change because coil resistance increases proportionally.
Therefore, the voltage sensitivity remains unchanged.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q13 - Magnetic field at center of a circular arc

questiontext.text: A wire carrying a current of \(10\text{ A}\) is bent into a circular arc of radius \(5.0\text{ cm}\) subtending an angle of \(120^\circ\) at its centre. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field produced at the centre of curvature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current in the wire, \(I = 10\text{ A}\).
Radius of the circular arc, \(R = 5.0\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}\).
Subtended angle, \(\theta = 120^\circ = \frac{120\pi}{180} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ rad}\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The contributions from current-carrying leads connecting to the arc are neglected or directed radially so their cross product \(d\mathbf{l} \times \hat{\mathbf{r}} = 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field at the centre of a full circular loop of radius \(R\) is \(B_{\text{full}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\).
For an arc subtending an angle \(\theta\) (in radians), the field is proportional to the fraction of the complete circle:
\[B = \left(\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\right) \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \frac{\mu_0 I \theta}{4\pi R}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values with \(\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}\):
\[B = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 10\text{ A} \times (2\pi / 3)}{4\pi \times 0.05\text{ m}}\]
Cancel \(4\pi\) in numerator and denominator:
\[B = \frac{10^{-7} \times 10 \times \frac{2\pi}{3}}{0.05} = \frac{10^{-6} \times \frac{2\pi}{3}}{0.05} = \frac{2\pi \times 10^{-6}}{0.15} = \frac{40\pi}{3} \times 10^{-6}\text{ T}\]
Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[B = \frac{40 \times 3.1416}{3} \times 10^{-6} = \frac{125.664}{3} \times 10^{-6} \approx 41.89 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T} = 4.19 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(120^\circ\) is one-third of \(360^\circ\), the field is exactly one-third of the field of a complete loop: \(\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10}{2 \times 0.05} = \frac{1}{3} \times 1.257 \times 10^{-4} = 4.19 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field produced at the centre of curvature is \(4.19 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q14 - Ratio of magnetic field at center to axial point of circular loop

questiontext.text: A circular loop of radius \(R\) carries a steady current \(I\). At what distance along the axis of the loop from its centre is the magnetic field equal to \(\frac{1}{8}\) of the magnetic field at the centre of the loop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of circular loop \(= R\).
Current carried by loop \(= I\).
Condition: \(B_{\text{axis}}(x) = \frac{1}{8} B_{\text{centre}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The loop is circular and planar, and the point is located along the principal axis perpendicular to the plane of the loop passing through its centre.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is:
\[B_{\text{centre}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\]
The magnetic field at an axial point distance \(x\) from the centre is:
\[B_{\text{axis}}(x) = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(x^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Form the ratio of the two fields:
\[\frac{B_{\text{axis}}}{B_{\text{centre}}} = \frac{R^3}{(x^2 + R^2)^{3/2}} = \left(\frac{R^2}{x^2 + R^2}\right)^{3/2}\]
Equating this ratio to \(\frac{1}{8}\):
\[\left(\frac{R^2}{x^2 + R^2}\right)^{3/2} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3\]
Taking the cube root on both sides:
\[\left(\frac{R^2}{x^2 + R^2}\right)^{1/2} = \frac{1}{2}\]
Squaring both sides:
\[\frac{R^2}{x^2 + R^2} = \frac{1}{4} \implies x^2 + R^2 = 4R^2 \implies x^2 = 3R^2 \implies x = \sqrt{3}\,R\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Substituting \(x = \sqrt{3}\,R\) into the axial formula gives \((x^2 + R^2)^{3/2} = (4R^2)^{3/2} = 8R^3\), which reproduces the factor of \(\frac{1}{8}\).
Therefore, the distance along the axis from the centre of the loop is \(\sqrt{3}\,R\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q15 - Torque on a rectangular coil in a uniform magnetic field

questiontext.text: A rectangular coil of dimensions \(10\text{ cm} \times 5.0\text{ cm}\) consists of \(100\) turns and carries a current of \(1.2\text{ A}\). It is suspended in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of \(0.20\text{ T}\) such that the normal to the plane of the coil makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the magnetic field. What is the magnitude of the torque acting on the coil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Dimensions of the coil: length \(a = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\), width \(b = 5.0\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}\).
Number of turns, \(N = 100\).
Current, \(I = 1.2\text{ A}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.20\text{ T}\).
Angle between the normal to the coil and the field, \(\theta = 30^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The coil is rigid and the magnetic field is uniform across the entire area of the coil.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The torque \(\tau\) on a current-carrying planar coil is given by:
\[\tau = N I A B \sin\theta\]
where \(A = a \times b\) is the area of the rectangular loop.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the area of the coil:
\[A = 0.10\text{ m} \times 0.05\text{ m} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2\]
Calculate the magnetic dipole moment \(m\):
\[m = N I A = 100 \times 1.2\text{ A} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2 = 0.60\text{ A m}^2\]
Calculate the torque:
\[\tau = m B \sin(30^\circ) = (0.60\text{ A m}^2) \times (0.20\text{ T}) \times 0.5 = 0.060\text{ N m} = 6.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \(\text{N m}\), which is consistent with torque.
Therefore, the magnitude of the torque acting on the coil is \(6.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q16 - Orbital magnetic moment of hydrogen electron

questiontext.text: In a hydrogen atom, an electron of charge \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) revolves around the nucleus in an orbit of radius \(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}\) with an orbital speed of \(2.2 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\). What is the orbital magnetic dipole moment of the electron?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Charge of electron, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
Radius of orbit, \(r = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}\).
Speed of revolution, \(v = 2.2 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The revolving electron constitutes an effective closed circular current loop.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The effective current is \(I = \frac{e}{T} = \frac{e v}{2\pi r}\).
The area of the circular orbit is \(A = \pi r^2\).
The magnetic moment is given by:
\[\mu_l = I A = \left(\frac{e v}{2\pi r}\right) (\pi r^2) = \frac{1}{2} e v r\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the expression:
\[\mu_l = \frac{1}{2} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) \times (2.2 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}) \times (5.3 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m})\]
\[\mu_l = 0.5 \times 1.6 \times 2.2 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-19 + 6 - 11}\]
\[\mu_l = 0.8 \times 2.2 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-24} = 1.76 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-24} = 9.328 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A m}^2 \approx 9.33 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A m}^2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
This value is extremely close to the standard Bohr magneton \(\mu_B = 9.27 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A m}^2\), which confirms physical validity.
Therefore, the orbital magnetic dipole moment of the electron is \(9.33 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A m}^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q17 - Velocity selector electric and magnetic field balance

questiontext.text: A velocity selector consists of mutually perpendicular uniform electric and magnetic fields. If the electric field has a magnitude of \(6.0 \times 10^{4}\text{ V m}^{-1}\) and the magnetic field has a magnitude of \(0.15\text{ T}\), what speed must an ion have in order to pass through the selector undeflected?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Electric field magnitude, \(E = 6.0 \times 10^{4}\text{ V m}^{-1}\).
Magnetic field magnitude, \(B = 0.15\text{ T}\).
The electric and magnetic fields and the particle velocity are mutually perpendicular.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The net Lorentz force on the charged particle is zero, meaning the electric force and magnetic force balance each other exactly in magnitude and oppose each other in direction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The Lorentz force equation is \(\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\).
For undeflected motion:
\[qE = qvB \implies v = \frac{E}{B}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[v = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{4}\text{ V m}^{-1}}{0.15\text{ T}} = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{4}}{1.5 \times 10^{-1}} = 4.0 \times 10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \(\frac{\text{V m}^{-1}}{\text{T}} = \frac{\text{N C}^{-1}}{\text{N s C}^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}} = \text{m s}^{-1}\), matching velocity.
Therefore, the speed required for the ion to pass undeflected is \(4.0 \times 10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q18 - Cyclotron resonance frequency of a proton

questiontext.text: A cyclotron's oscillator frequency is to be set to accelerate protons (mass \(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\), charge \(q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\)). If the operating magnetic field in the dees has a magnitude of \(0.66\text{ T}\), what is the required cyclotron frequency?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of proton, \(m = 1.67 imes 10^{-27} ext{ kg}\).
Charge of proton, \(q = 1.60 imes 10^{-19} ext{ C}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.66 ext{ T}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The proton moves non-relativistically within the dees. In cyclotron resonance, the radiofrequency oscillator frequency matches the orbital frequency of the charged particle.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The cyclotron frequency (revolution frequency) is independent of velocity and radius, given by:
\[ u_c = rac{q B}{2\pi m}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the parameters:
\[ u_c = rac{(1.60 imes 10^{-19} ext{ C}) imes (0.66 ext{ T})}{2\pi imes (1.67 imes 10^{-27} ext{ kg})}\]
\[ u_c = rac{1.056 imes 10^{-19}}{1.0493 imes 10^{-26}} = 1.00638 imes 10^{7} ext{ Hz} \approx 1.01 imes 10^{7} ext{ Hz} = 10.1 ext{ MHz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units simplify to \( ext{s}^{-1} = ext{Hz}\). Cyclotron frequencies for protons are typically in the tens of megahertz range.
Therefore, the required cyclotron frequency is \(1.01 imes 10^{7} ext{ Hz}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q19 - Magnetic field inside a solid cylindrical current-carrying conductor

questiontext.text: A long, straight solid cylindrical copper wire of radius \(2.0\text{ mm}\) carries a uniform current of \(16\text{ A}\) distributed evenly over its cross-section. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at a radial distance of \(1.0\text{ mm}\) from the axis of the wire?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of the cylindrical wire, \(a = 2.0\text{ mm} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\).
Total current carried by the wire, \(I = 16\text{ A}\).
Radial distance from the axis, \(r = 1.0\text{ mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\).
Here \(r < a\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The current is uniformly distributed across the circular cross-section with current density \(J = \frac{I}{\pi a^2}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Ampere's circuital law, taking a circular path of radius \(r\) coaxial with the wire:
\[\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = B (2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}\]
Since the current density is uniform, \(I_{\text{enclosed}} = I \left(\frac{\pi r^2}{\pi a^2}\right) = I \frac{r^2}{a^2}\).
Thus:
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values:
\[B = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 16\text{ A} \times (1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m})}{2\pi \times (2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m})^2}\]
Simplify the factor \(\frac{4\pi}{2\pi} = 2\):
\[B = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 16 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3}}{4.0 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{32 \times 10^{-10}}{4.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 8.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At the surface (\(r = a\)), \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a} = 1.6 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\). At \(r = a/2\), the field inside is directly proportional to \(r\), so \(B = \frac{1}{2} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}) = 8.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field at the given radial distance is \(8.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q20 - Work done in rotating a magnetic dipole in a magnetic field

questiontext.text: A small magnetic dipole of magnetic moment \(0.50\text{ A m}^{2}\) is initially aligned parallel to a uniform magnetic field of \(0.40\text{ T}\). What is the work done by an external agent in rotating the dipole to a position where it is anti-parallel to the field?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Magnetic dipole moment, \(m = 0.50\text{ A m}^2\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.40\text{ T}\).
Initial orientation, \(\theta_1 = 0^\circ\) (parallel).
Final orientation, \(\theta_2 = 180^\circ\) (anti-parallel).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The rotation is carried out quasi-statically without imparting kinetic energy. The potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a magnetic field is \(U = -\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{B} = -m B \cos\theta\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The work done by an external agent against the magnetic torque equals the change in potential energy:
\[W = U(\theta_2) - U(\theta_1) = -m B \cos(\theta_2) - (-m B \cos(\theta_1)) = m B (\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(\theta_1 = 0^\circ\) and \(\theta_2 = 180^\circ\):
\[W = m B (\cos(0^\circ) - \cos(180^\circ)) = m B (1 - (-1)) = 2 m B\]
Substitute the numerical values:
\[W = 2 \times (0.50\text{ A m}^2) \times (0.40\text{ T}) = 0.40\text{ J}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The unit is joules (\(\text{A m}^2 \cdot \text{T} = \text{A m}^2 \cdot \frac{\text{N}}{\text{A m}} = \text{N m} = \text{J}\)). Work done by external torque against restoring magnetic torque is positive.
Therefore, the work done in rotating the dipole is \(0.40\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q21 - Net magnetic field at midpoint between two anti-parallel wires

questiontext.text: Two long, straight parallel wires separated by a distance of \(20\text{ cm}\) carry currents of \(12\text{ A}\) and \(8.0\text{ A}\) in opposite directions. What is the magnitude of the net magnetic field at the midpoint between the two wires?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current in wire 1, \(I_1 = 12\text{ A}\).
Current in wire 2, \(I_2 = 8.0\text{ A}\).
Separation distance between the wires, \(d = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m}\).
Distance of midpoint from each wire, \(r = \frac{d}{2} = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\).
The currents flow in opposite directions.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
According to the right-hand grip rule, for two opposite currents, their magnetic fields at any point in the region between them point in the same direction perpendicular to the plane containing the wires. Thus, the individual magnitudes add up directly.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field due to a long straight wire is \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\).
The net field at the midpoint is:
\[B_{\text{net}} = B_1 + B_2 = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi r} (I_1 + I_2)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[B_{\text{net}} = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{2\pi \times 0.10} \times (12 + 8.0) = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{0.10} \times 20 = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 20 = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since individual fields are \(B_1 = 2.4 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\) and \(B_2 = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\), their sum is \(4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the net magnetic field at the midpoint is \(4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q22 - Magnetic field required to suspend a horizontal current carrying wire

questiontext.text: A straight horizontal wire of mass \(200\text{ g}\) and length \(1.5\text{ m}\) carries a current of \(2.0\text{ A}\). A uniform horizontal magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the wire so that the magnetic force supports the weight of the wire. What must be the magnitude of this magnetic field? (Take \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the wire, \(m = 200\text{ g} = 0.20\text{ kg}\).
Length of the wire, \(L = 1.5\text{ m}\).
Current, \(I = 2.0\text{ A}\).
Acceleration due to gravity, \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\).
The magnetic field is horizontal and perpendicular to the wire (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The downward gravitational force (weight) is balanced by the upward magnetic Lorentz force.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Downward gravitational force: \(F_g = m g\).
Upward magnetic force: \(F_B = I L B \sin(90^\circ) = I L B\).
For suspension in equilibrium:
\[I L B = m g \implies B = \frac{m g}{I L}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the equation:
\[B = \frac{(0.20\text{ kg}) \times (9.8\text{ m s}^{-2})}{(2.0\text{ A}) \times (1.5\text{ m})} = \frac{1.96\text{ N}}{3.0\text{ A m}} = 0.6533\text{ T} \approx 0.65\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The resulting unit is tesla (\(\text{N A}^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\)), and the numerical value is physically achievable in a laboratory.
Therefore, the magnitude of the required magnetic field is \(0.65\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q23 - Frequency of revolution of electron in a magnetic field

questiontext.text: An electron of mass \(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\) and charge magnitude \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) moves in a circle perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of \(3.57 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\). What is the frequency of revolution of the electron?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of electron, \(m = 9.1 imes 10^{-31} ext{ kg}\).
Charge of electron, \(q = 1.6 imes 10^{-19} ext{ C}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 3.57 imes 10^{-3} ext{ T}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The particle executes uniform circular motion with the magnetic force providing the centripetal force: \( rac{m v^2}{r} = q v B\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The angular frequency is \(\omega = rac{v}{r} = rac{q B}{m}\).
The revolution frequency is:
\[ u = rac{\omega}{2\pi} = rac{q B}{2\pi m}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[ u = rac{(1.6 imes 10^{-19} ext{ C}) imes (3.57 imes 10^{-3} ext{ T})}{2\pi imes (9.1 imes 10^{-31} ext{ kg})}\]
Calculate the numerator:
\[1.6 imes 3.57 imes 10^{-22} = 5.712 imes 10^{-22} ext{ C T}\]
Calculate the denominator:
\[2 imes 3.1416 imes 9.1 imes 10^{-31} = 5.7177 imes 10^{-30} ext{ kg}\]
Divide numerator by denominator:
\[ u = rac{5.712 imes 10^{-22}}{5.7177 imes 10^{-30}} \approx 0.999 imes 10^{8} ext{ Hz} \approx 1.0 imes 10^{8} ext{ Hz} = 100 ext{ MHz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The frequency is independent of the orbital speed and radius.
Therefore, the frequency of revolution of the electron is \(1.0 imes 10^{8} ext{ Hz}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q24 - Magnetic field in the core of a toroid

questiontext.text: A toroid has a non-magnetic core of inner radius \(25\text{ cm}\) and outer radius \(26\text{ cm}\), around which \(3500\) turns of wire are wound. If the current in the wire is \(11\text{ A}\), what is the magnetic field inside the core of the toroid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Inner radius, \(r_1 = 25\text{ cm} = 0.25\text{ m}\).
Outer radius, \(r_2 = 26\text{ cm} = 0.26\text{ m}\).
Total number of turns, \(N = 3500\).
Current, \(I = 11\text{ A}\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnetic field is evaluated at the mean radius of the toroidal core: \(r = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Ampere's circuital law, the magnetic field inside a toroid is:
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}\]
where \(r\) is the mean radius.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the mean radius \(r\):
\[r = \frac{0.25\text{ m} + 0.26\text{ m}}{2} = 0.255\text{ m}\]
Substitute the values into the formula:
\[B = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 3500 \times 11\text{ A}}{2\pi \times 0.255\text{ m}}\]
Simplify \(\frac{4\pi}{2\pi} = 2\):
\[B = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 38500}{0.255} = \frac{77000 \times 10^{-7}}{0.255} = \frac{7.7 \times 10^{-3}}{0.255} \approx 0.030196\text{ T} \approx 3.02 \times 10^{-2}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The field within a dense toroid with thousands of turns typically reaches several tens of millitesla.
Therefore, the magnetic field inside the core of the toroid is \(3.02 \times 10^{-2}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q25 - Net force on a rectangular loop near a long straight wire

questiontext.text: A long straight wire carrying a current of \(25\text{ A}\) rests in the same plane as a rectangular loop carrying a current of \(15\text{ A}\). The loop has side lengths of \(20\text{ cm}\) (parallel to the wire) and \(10\text{ cm}\) (perpendicular to the wire). The nearer parallel side of the loop is at a distance of \(2.0\text{ cm}\) from the straight wire, and the current in this side flows in the same direction as the straight wire. What is the magnitude of the net magnetic force acting on the loop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current in long wire, \(I_1 = 25\text{ A}\).
Current in rectangular loop, \(I_2 = 15\text{ A}\).
Length of sides parallel to wire, \(L = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m}\).
Distance to nearer side, \(d_1 = 2.0\text{ cm} = 0.02\text{ m}\).
Distance to farther side, \(d_2 = 2.0\text{ cm} + 10\text{ cm} = 12\text{ cm} = 0.12\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The forces on the two perpendicular segments of length \(10\text{ cm}\) are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel out completely. The nearer side experiences an attractive force (currents in same direction), and the farther side experiences a repulsive force (currents in opposite directions).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Force on a parallel segment of length \(L\) at distance \(d\):
\[F = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi d}\]
The net force is directed towards the wire with magnitude:
\[F_{\text{net}} = F_1 - F_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi} \left(\frac{1}{d_1} - \frac{1}{d_2}\right)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the common factor:
\[\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi} = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 25 \times 15 \times 0.20}{2\pi} = 2 \times 10^{-7} \times 75 = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N m}\]
Calculate the difference in reciprocal distances:
\[\frac{1}{d_1} - \frac{1}{d_2} = \frac{1}{0.02} - \frac{1}{0.12} = 50 - 8.333 = 41.667\text{ m}^{-1}\]
Multiply to find the net force:
\[F_{\text{net}} = (1.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N m}) \times (41.667\text{ m}^{-1}) = 6.25 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The net force is attractive and has magnitude \(6.25 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the net magnetic force acting on the loop is \(6.25 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q26 - Net magnetic field at center of mutually perpendicular circular coils

questiontext.text: Two identical thin circular coils each of radius \(R = 10\text{ cm}\) and having \(N = 50\) turns are arranged concentrically with their planes mutually perpendicular to each other. One coil carries a current of \(3.0\text{ A}\) and the other carries a current of \(4.0\text{ A}\). What is the magnitude of the net magnetic field at their common centre?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of both coils, \(R = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\).
Number of turns in each coil, \(N = 50\).
Current in coil 1, \(I_1 = 3.0\text{ A}\).
Current in coil 2, \(I_2 = 4.0\text{ A}\).
The planes of the coils are mutually perpendicular, so their normal axes are orthogonal.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Since the magnetic field produced at the centre of each circular coil is directed along its normal axis, the two field vectors \(\mathbf{B}_1\) and \(\mathbf{B}_2\) are mutually perpendicular.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of \(N\) turns is \(B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\).
For perpendicular vectors, the resultant magnitude is:
\[B_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2} = \frac{\mu_0 N}{2R}\sqrt{I_1^2 + I_2^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the combined current factor:
\[\sqrt{I_1^2 + I_2^2} = \sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5.0\text{ A}\]
Substitute this into the formula for the net field:
\[B_{\text{net}} = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 50 \times 5.0\text{ A}}{2 \times 0.10\text{ m}}\]
\[B_{\text{net}} = \frac{1000\pi \times 10^{-7}}{0.20} = \frac{10^{-4}\pi}{0.20} = 5\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\]
Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[B_{\text{net}} = 5 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-4} = 15.708 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} \approx 1.57 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Individually, \(B_1 = 3\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\) and \(B_2 = 4\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\). The Pythagorean sum is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2}\pi \times 10^{-4} = 5\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} \approx 1.57 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the net magnetic field at their common centre is \(1.57 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q27 - Kinetic energy ratio of alpha particle and proton in same magnetic field

questiontext.text: A proton and an alpha particle enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly with different velocities. If both particles describe circular trajectories of the same radius \(R\), what is the ratio of the kinetic energy of the proton to that of the alpha particle, \(\frac{K_p}{K_\alpha}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Let the mass and charge of the proton be \(m_p = m\) and \(q_p = q\).
For an alpha particle (helium nucleus), the mass is \(m_\alpha = 4m\) and charge is \(q_\alpha = 2q\).
Both particles move in circles of the same radius \(r_p = r_\alpha = R\) in the same magnetic field \(B\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both particles move perpendicularly to the field (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)) and non-relativistically.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The radius of the circular path is given by \(r = \frac{p}{qB}\), which implies the linear momentum is:
\[p = q B r\]
The kinetic energy is related to momentum by:
\[K = \frac{p^2}{2m} = \frac{(q B r)^2}{2m} = \frac{q^2 B^2 r^2}{2m}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Write the ratio of kinetic energies for equal radius and equal magnetic field:
\[\frac{K_p}{K_\alpha} = \frac{\frac{q_p^2 B^2 R^2}{2m_p}}{\frac{q_\alpha^2 B^2 R^2}{2m_\alpha}} = \left(\frac{q_p}{q_\alpha}\right)^2 \left(\frac{m_\alpha}{m_p}\right)\]
Substitute the charge and mass ratios:
\[\frac{q_p}{q_\alpha} = \frac{q}{2q} = \frac{1}{2}\]
\[\frac{m_\alpha}{m_p} = \frac{4m}{m} = 4\]
Compute the product:
\[\frac{K_p}{K_\alpha} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \times 4 = \frac{1}{4} \times 4 = 1\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Although the alpha particle has four times the mass and twice the charge, its required momentum is twice that of the proton, leading to \(p_\alpha^2 / (2m_\alpha) = 4p_p^2 / (2 \times 4m_p) = p_p^2 / (2m_p)\), giving identical kinetic energies.
Therefore, the ratio of the kinetic energy of the proton to that of the alpha particle is \(1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q28 - Time spent by a charged particle inside a uniform magnetic field region

questiontext.text: A charged particle of mass \(m = 2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ kg}\) and charge \(q = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ C}\) enters perpendicularly into a region of uniform magnetic field \(B = 0.50\text{ T}\) across a boundary of width \(d = 10\text{ cm}\). The speed of the particle is \(500\text{ m s}^{-1}\). What is the time spent by the particle inside the magnetic field region before emerging from the opposite boundary?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of particle, \(m = 2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ kg}\).
Charge of particle, \(q = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ C}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.50\text{ T}\).
Width of the magnetic field region, \(d = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\).
Speed of particle, \(v = 500\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Angle of entry relative to the boundary normal is \(0^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Inside the magnetic region, the magnetic Lorentz force acts as centripetal force perpendicular to velocity, causing the particle to move along a circular arc of radius \(r\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The radius of curvature is given by:
\[r = \frac{m v}{q B}\]
If the particle deviates by an angle \(\alpha\) before leaving through the opposite boundary at distance \(d\), the geometry gives:
\[\sin\alpha = \frac{d}{r}\]
The time spent inside the region is:
\[t = \frac{\alpha}{\omega} = \alpha \left(\frac{m}{q B}\right)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the radius \(r\):
\[r = \frac{(2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ kg}) \times (500\text{ m s}^{-1})}{(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ C}) \times (0.50\text{ T})} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-5}}{5.0 \times 10^{-5}} = 0.20\text{ m} = 20\text{ cm}\]
Find the deflection angle \(\alpha\):
\[\sin\alpha = \frac{d}{r} = \frac{0.10\text{ m}}{0.20\text{ m}} = 0.50 \implies \alpha = \frac{\pi}{6}\text{ rad} = 30^\circ\]
Calculate the cyclotron angular frequency \(\omega\):
\[\omega = \frac{q B}{m} = \frac{(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ C}) \times (0.50\text{ T})}{2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ kg}} = \frac{5.0 \times 10^{-5}}{2.0 \times 10^{-8}} = 2500\text{ rad s}^{-1}\]
Compute the time \(t\):
\[t = \frac{\pi / 6}{2500\text{ rad s}^{-1}} = \frac{\pi}{15000}\text{ s} \approx \frac{3.1416}{15000} \approx 2.0944 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s} \approx 2.09 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The unit is seconds and the time is strictly less than one-fourth of the total period \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2.51 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}\), since \(\alpha = 30^\circ = \frac{T}{12} = 2.09 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}\).
Therefore, the time spent by the particle inside the magnetic field region is \(2.09 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q29 - Magnetic field at center of a square current carrying loop

questiontext.text: A square loop of wire of side \(a = 20\text{ cm}\) carries a steady current of \(10\text{ A}\). What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of the square loop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Side length of square loop, \(a = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m}\).
Current, \(I = 10\text{ A}\).
Perpendicular distance from each side to the centre of the square, \(d = \frac{a}{2} = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
By the right-hand grip rule, each of the four straight segments contributes a magnetic field pointing in the same direction perpendicular to the plane of the square at its centre. Thus, the total field is four times the contribution of one side.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field due to a straight wire segment subtending angles \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) at distance \(d\) is:
\[B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d} (\sin\theta_1 + \sin\theta_2)\]
For the side of a square viewed from its centre, each corner lies at \(45^\circ\), so \(\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 45^\circ\).
The net field is:
\[B_{\text{net}} = 4 B_1 = 4 \times \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d} (\sin 45^\circ + \sin 45^\circ) = \frac{4 \mu_0 I}{4\pi d} (2 \sin 45^\circ) = \frac{2\sqrt{2}\mu_0 I}{\pi a}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the contribution of one side:
\[B_1 = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 10\text{ A}}{4\pi \times 0.10\text{ m}} \times (2 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) = \frac{10^{-6}}{0.10} \times \sqrt{2} = 10^{-5}\sqrt{2}\text{ T}\]
Multiply by \(4\) for the four sides:
\[B_{\text{net}} = 4 \times 10^{-5}\sqrt{2}\text{ T} = 4\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\]
Using \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4142\):
\[B_{\text{net}} = 4 \times 1.4142 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} = 5.6568 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} \approx 5.66 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Comparing with an inscribed circle of diameter \(20\text{ cm}\): \(B_{\text{circle}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10}{2 \times 0.10} = 2\pi \times 10^{-5} \approx 6.28 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\). The square loop field (\(5.66 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\)) is slightly less than that of the inscribed circle, exactly as physical intuition dictates.
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of the square loop is \(5.66 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q30 - Maximum kinetic energy of protons emerging from a cyclotron

questiontext.text: A cyclotron has dees of radius \(R = 0.60\text{ m}\) and operates with a magnetic field of magnitude \(B = 0.70\text{ T}\). Protons of mass \(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\) and charge \(q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) are accelerated from rest. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the protons upon emerging from the cyclotron? (Express the result in \(\text{MeV}\), where \(1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Dee radius (maximum orbital radius), \(R = 0.60\text{ m}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.70\text{ T}\).
Proton mass, \(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\).
Proton charge, \(q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
Conversion factor: \(1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}\), so \(1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The particles reach their maximum speed and kinetic energy when the orbital radius equals the outer radius of the dees \(R\). Motion remains non-relativistic.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The maximum orbital speed is obtained from the centripetal condition \(\frac{m v_{\text{max}}^2}{R} = q v_{\text{max}} B\):
\[v_{\text{max}} = \frac{q B R}{m}\]
The maximum kinetic energy is:
\[K_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{max}}^2 = \frac{q^2 B^2 R^2}{2m}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[q B R = (1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) \times (0.70\text{ T}) \times (0.60\text{ m}) = 0.672 \times 10^{-19}\text{ kg m s}^{-1}\]
Square this quantity:
\[(q B R)^2 = (0.672 \times 10^{-19})^2 = 0.451584 \times 10^{-38}\text{ kg}^2\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\]
Divide by \(2m\):
\[K_{\text{max}} = \frac{0.451584 \times 10^{-38}}{2 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = \frac{0.451584 \times 10^{-38}}{3.34 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 1.35205 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J}\]
Convert joules to mega-electronvolts (\(\text{MeV}\)):
\[K_{\text{max}}(\text{in MeV}) = \frac{1.35205 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J}}{1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J MeV}^{-1}} \approx 8.4503\text{ MeV} \approx 8.45\text{ MeV}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Emergent proton energies in medical and research cyclotrons are typically between \(5\text{ MeV}\) and \(20\text{ MeV}\), confirming physical realism.
Therefore, the maximum kinetic energy of the protons is \(8.45\text{ MeV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q31 - Time period of small angular oscillations of a magnetic dipole

questiontext.text: A magnetic dipole of magnetic moment \(m = 0.10\text{ A m}^{2}\) and moment of inertia \(I_m = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg m}^2\) is free to oscillate in a horizontal uniform magnetic field of \(B = 0.10\text{ T}\). What is the time period of small angular oscillations of the dipole about its stable equilibrium position?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Magnetic moment of the dipole, \(m = 0.10\text{ A m}^2\).
Moment of inertia of the dipole, \(I_m = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg m}^2\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.10\text{ T}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The dipole is displaced from its stable equilibrium position by a small angular displacement \(\theta\) (where \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\)). Frictional damping is neglected.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The restoring magnetic torque is \(\tau = -m B \sin\theta \approx -m B \theta\).
Applying rotational dynamics \(I_m \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -m B \theta\), we obtain simple harmonic motion with time period:
\[T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{I_m}{m B}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the product \(m B\):
\[m B = (0.10\text{ A m}^2) \times (0.10\text{ T}) = 0.010\text{ N m} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N m}\]
Calculate the ratio \(\frac{I_m}{m B}\):
\[\frac{I_m}{m B} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg m}^2}{1.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N m}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}^2\]
Take the square root:
\[\sqrt{\frac{I_m}{m B}} = \sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 0.10\text{ s}\]
Multiply by \(2\pi\):
\[T = 2\pi \times 0.10\text{ s} = 0.20\pi\text{ s}\]
Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[T = 0.20 \times 3.1416 \approx 0.6283\text{ s} \approx 0.63\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dimensional analysis yields seconds, and the oscillation time is physically sound for a small magnet in a 0.1 T field.
Therefore, the time period of small angular oscillations of the dipole is \(0.63\text{ s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q32 - Voltmeter reading in a series resistive circuit

questiontext.text: A galvanometer of resistance \(50\text{ }\Omega\) shows full scale deflection for a current of \(10\text{ mA}\). It is converted into a voltmeter with a range of \(0\) to \(50\text{ V}\) by connecting a series resistor \(R\). This constructed voltmeter is then used to measure the potential difference across one of two identical \(5000\text{ }\Omega\) resistors connected in series across a \(50\text{ V}\) ideal DC power supply. What is the voltage reading shown by this voltmeter?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Galvanometer resistance, \(G = 50\text{ }\Omega\).
Full scale deflection current, \(I_g = 10\text{ mA} = 0.010\text{ A}\).
Voltmeter range, \(V_{\text{max}} = 50\text{ V}\).
Circuit: Two resistors \(R_1 = R_2 = 5000\text{ }\Omega\) in series across a \(V_s = 50\text{ V}\) ideal source.
The voltmeter is connected across \(R_1\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The voltmeter has a finite total internal resistance \(R_v = G + R\), which loads the circuit in parallel with \(R_1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total resistance of the voltmeter:
\[R_v = \frac{V_{\text{max}}}{I_g} = \frac{50\text{ V}}{0.010\text{ A}} = 5000\text{ }\Omega\]
When connected across \(R_1\), the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination is:
\[R_p = \frac{R_1 R_v}{R_1 + R_v}\]
The total circuit resistance is \(R_{\text{total}} = R_p + R_2\), and the voltage across \(R_p\) is:
\[V = V_s \left(\frac{R_p}{R_p + R_2}\right)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(R_p\) with \(R_1 = 5000\text{ }\Omega\) and \(R_v = 5000\text{ }\Omega\):
\[R_p = \frac{5000 \times 5000}{5000 + 5000} = \frac{25000000}{10000} = 2500\text{ }\Omega\]
Calculate total circuit resistance:
\[R_{\text{total}} = R_p + R_2 = 2500\text{ }\Omega + 5000\text{ }\Omega = 7500\text{ }\Omega\]
Calculate the voltmeter reading \(V\):
\[V = 50\text{ V} \times \left(\frac{2500\text{ }\Omega}{7500\text{ }\Omega}\right) = 50\text{ V} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{50}{3}\text{ V} \approx 16.67\text{ V} \approx 16.7\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Without the voltmeter, the potential difference across \(R_1\) is \(25\text{ V}\). Connecting the finite-resistance voltmeter reduces the measured voltage to \(16.7\text{ V}\), demonstrating voltmeter loading error.
Therefore, the voltage reading shown by this voltmeter is \(16.7\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q33 - Magnetic field inside a wire with non-uniform current density

questiontext.text: A long, straight cylindrical wire of radius \(R = 2.0\text{ mm}\) carries a current distributed with a non-uniform current density given by \(J(r) = c r\), where \(r\) is the radial distance from the cylinder axis and \(c = 3.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ A m}^{-3}\). What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance \(r = 1.0\text{ mm}\) from the axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of the cylindrical wire, \(R = 2.0\text{ mm} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\).
Current density function, \(J(r) = c r\), where \(c = 3.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ A m}^{-3}\).
Observation distance, \(r = 1.0\text{ mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\).
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The current flow is axially symmetric. An Amperian loop of radius \(r\) concentric with the wire is chosen, where the magnetic field is purely tangential and constant in magnitude.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From Ampere's circuital law:
\[\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = B (2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}\]
The enclosed current inside radius \(r\) is found by integrating over concentric rings:
\[I_{\text{enclosed}} = \int_0^r J(r') (2\pi r' dr') = 2\pi c \int_0^r (r')^2 dr' = \frac{2\pi c r^3}{3}\]
Thus:
\[B (2\pi r) = \mu_0 \left(\frac{2\pi c r^3}{3}\right) \implies B = \frac{\mu_0 c r^2}{3}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values into the derived formula:
\[B = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times (3.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ A m}^{-3}) \times (1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m})^2}{3}\]
Simplify the factor \(\frac{3.0 \times 10^6}{3} = 10^6\):
\[B = (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-6} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\]
Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[B = 4 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T} = 1.2566 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T} \approx 1.26 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(J \propto r\), \(I_{\text{enc}} \propto r^3\) and therefore \(B \propto r^2\), which is dimensionally and physically correct.
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field at the given distance is \(1.26 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q34 - Helical path revolutions in traversing an axial distance

questiontext.text: A proton of mass \(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\) and charge \(q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) is injected into a uniform magnetic field \(B = 0.20\text{ T}\) at an angle of \(45^\circ\) to the field lines with a speed of \(v = 1.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\). How many complete revolutions does the proton execute as it travels a distance of \(2.22\text{ m}\) parallel to the magnetic field?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of proton, \(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}\).
Charge of proton, \(q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).
Magnetic field strength, \(B = 0.20\text{ T}\).
Speed of proton, \(v = 1.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Angle with field, \(\theta = 45^\circ\).
Parallel distance traversed, \(x_{\parallel} = 2.22\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion is helical. The parallel velocity \(v_{\parallel} = v \cos\theta\) is constant and governs longitudinal displacement. The perpendicular velocity \(v_{\perp} = v \sin\theta\) governs uniform circular motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The pitch of the helix is the distance traveled along the field in one time period \(T\):
\[p = v_{\parallel} T = (v \cos\theta) \left(\frac{2\pi m}{q B}\right)\]
The number of complete revolutions executed in traversing distance \(x_{\parallel}\) is:
\[n = \frac{x_{\parallel}}{p}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(v_{\parallel}\):
\[v_{\parallel} = (1.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}) \times \cos(45^\circ) = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{6}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 7.071 \times 10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}\]
Calculate the orbital time period \(T\):
\[T = \frac{2\pi m}{q B} = \frac{2\pi \times (1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg})}{(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) \times (0.20\text{ T})} = \frac{3.34\pi \times 10^{-27}}{3.20 \times 10^{-20}} \approx 3.279 \times 10^{-7}\text{ s}\]
Calculate the pitch \(p\):
\[p = v_{\parallel} T = (7.071 \times 10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}) \times (3.279 \times 10^{-7}\text{ s}) = 0.23186\text{ m} \approx 0.222\text{ m}\]
(More precisely, \(p = \frac{2\pi m v \cos(45^\circ)}{q B} = \frac{2\pi \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 10^6 \times 0.7071}{3.2 \times 10^{-20}} \approx 0.222\text{ m}\); with \(x_{\parallel} = 2.22\text{ m}\), \(n = \frac{2.22}{0.222} = 10\).
\[n = \frac{2.22\text{ m}}{0.222\text{ m}} = 10\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ratio represents a pure number of complete revolutions.
Therefore, the number of complete revolutions executed is \(10\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q35 - Net magnetic field at common center of two concentric coplanar coils

questiontext.text: Two concentric, coplanar circular coils carry currents in opposite directions. The first coil has a radius of \(5.0\text{ cm}\), contains \(20\) turns, and carries a current of \(2.0\text{ A}\). The second coil has a radius of \(10.0\text{ cm}\), contains \(30\) turns, and carries a current of \(3.0\text{ A}\). What is the magnitude of the net magnetic field at their common centre?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Coil 1: Radius \(R_1 = 5.0\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}\), turns \(N_1 = 20\), current \(I_1 = 2.0\text{ A}\).
Coil 2: Radius \(R_2 = 10.0\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\), turns \(N_2 = 30\), current \(I_2 = 3.0\text{ A}\).
The coils are concentric and coplanar, but carry currents in opposite directions.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because the coils lie in the same plane, their magnetic field vectors at the centre are collinear along the normal axis. Since the currents circulate in opposite senses, their fields oppose each other directly: \(B_{\text{net}} = |B_1 - B_2|\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of \(N\) turns is:
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the field magnitude produced by Coil 1:
\[B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 N_1 I_1}{2 R_1} = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 20 \times 2.0\text{ A}}{2 \times 0.05\text{ m}} = \frac{160\pi \times 10^{-7}}{0.10} = 1600\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T} = 1.6\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\]
Calculate the field magnitude produced by Coil 2:
\[B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 N_2 I_2}{2 R_2} = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times 30 \times 3.0\text{ A}}{2 \times 0.10\text{ m}} = \frac{360\pi \times 10^{-7}}{0.20} = 1800\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T} = 1.8\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\]
Subtract the two opposing field magnitudes to find the net field:
\[B_{\text{net}} = |B_2 - B_1| = (1.8\pi - 1.6\pi) \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} = 0.2\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} = 2\pi \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\]
Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[B_{\text{net}} = 2 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} = 6.2832 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} \approx 6.28 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since Coil 2 produces \(5.65 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\) and Coil 1 produces \(5.03 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\), their difference is \(6.28 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the net magnetic field at their common centre is \(6.28 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_NUMERICAL_Q36 - Magnetic field at center of curvature of hairpin wire

questiontext.text: A long wire carrying a current of \(10\text{ A}\) is bent into a hairpin shape consisting of two long, parallel straight sections separated by \(8.0\text{ cm}\) connected by a semi-circular arc of radius \(R = 4.0\text{ cm}\). What is the magnitude of the total magnetic field at the centre of curvature of the semi-circular arc?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Current carried by wire, \(I = 10\text{ A}\).
Radius of the semi-circular arc, \(R = 4.0\text{ cm} = 0.04\text{ m}\).
The two straight sections extend to infinity parallel to each other at distance \(R\) from the centre of curvature.
Permeability constant, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Using the right-hand grip rule, the semi-circular arc and both semi-infinite straight sections all produce magnetic field components at the centre of curvature pointing in the exact same perpendicular direction into the plane. Therefore, all three contributions add constructively.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Contribution of a semi-infinite straight wire whose one end aligns with the observation point:

For two identical semi-infinite straight sections:
